title: A Journey I Will Never Forget
paragraphs: Last summer, Rustam Seilov travelled from Uralsk to Almaty by train — a journey of nearly thirty hours. He was travelling alone for the first time in his life, and he was carrying everything he owned in a large blue rucksack and a smaller bag that kept falling off his shoulder. The train left Uralsk station at 6:15 in the morning. Rustam was standing on the platform at 5:50, eating a sandwich from the station café and trying not to look nervous.

The compartment had four berths. When Rustam arrived, an elderly woman called Apai Raushan was already sitting in the corner, reading a thick novel. A middle-aged man was sleeping across from her, snoring quietly. The fourth berth was empty. Rustam put his large rucksack under the bed and climbed up to his top bunk. He was planning to sleep for the first few hours, but his mind was racing too fast.

As the train was moving through the flat steppe of western Kazakhstan, Rustam was thinking about everything that was waiting for him in Almaty — his new university, his dormitory room, the people he hadn't met yet. He had never been to Almaty before. In his imagination, it was enormous, loud, and completely overwhelming. He lay on his bunk and stared at the ceiling.

At around noon, Apai Raushan put down her novel and looked up at him. "Are you going to university?" she asked. Rustam was surprised — he hadn't said a word since he got on the train. He sat up and nodded. "Almaty," he said. She smiled. "I went there in 1978. My first time. I was shaking the whole way." Rustam laughed. "I'm not shaking," he said. She looked at him with kind eyes. "You are on the inside."

They talked for the rest of the afternoon. Apai Raushan had been a maths teacher for thirty-five years in a small town near Shymkent. She was travelling to Almaty to visit her daughter and meet her new granddaughter for the first time. She told Rustam stories about her own student years — about sharing a dormitory with seven other women, about studying for exams in a coat because there was no heating, about the friend who became her husband.

When the train pulled into Almaty station at noon the next day, Rustam was standing at the window watching the city appear. Buildings were rising on both sides of the track. The streets were busy. It was enormous. But he wasn't frightened anymore. Apai Raushan was standing beside him, also looking out. "Ready?" she asked. He nodded. "Ready," he said.

He took her phone number and put it in his contacts under "Apai Raushan — Train to Almaty." He called her three months later to tell her he had passed all his first-semester exams. She said she already knew he would. He still doesn't entirely understand how she could have known that — but he believes she was right.

When people ask Rustam about his best memory from his first year at university, he doesn't talk about his grades or his exams. He talks about a thirty-hour train journey and an old woman who saw something in him that he couldn't yet see in himself. "That train journey," he always says, "was the first day I started becoming the person I want to be."

dialogue.speaker: Kamila
dialogue.text: Rustam, you've told this story about the train journey before, but I never get tired of it.

dialogue.speaker: Rustam
dialogue.text: I think about Apai Raushan sometimes. I hope she's well.

dialogue.speaker: Kamila
dialogue.text: Did you ever call her again after that first time?

dialogue.speaker: Rustam
dialogue.text: Yes, on New Year's Eve. She remembered everything I'd told her about my courses.

dialogue.speaker: Kamila
dialogue.text: That's wonderful. Do you think you would have felt so calm arriving in Almaty without her?

dialogue.speaker: Rustam
dialogue.text: Absolutely not. I was terrified. That conversation completely changed how I felt.

dialogue.speaker: Kamila
dialogue.text: It's interesting — a stranger on a train. You never know who you'll meet.

dialogue.speaker: Rustam
dialogue.text: That's what I think too. Every journey is actually two journeys — the one outside and the one inside.

vocab.definition: a bag you carry on your back, especially when travelling
vocab.example: Rustam was carrying everything he owned in a large blue rucksack.

vocab.definition: a sleeping place on a train or ship
vocab.example: The compartment had four berths — Rustam took the top bunk.

vocab.definition: a separate division of a railway carriage
vocab.example: There were four people in the train compartment.

vocab.definition: a large area of flat land with no trees, common in Central Asia
vocab.example: The train was moving through the flat steppe of western Kazakhstan.

vocab.definition: very great in amount, or very difficult to deal with
vocab.example: In his imagination, Almaty was enormous and completely overwhelming.
Rustam was terrified about arriving in Almaty alone.

vocab.definition: very large in size or amount
vocab.example: Almaty was enormous — buildings were rising on both sides of the track.

vocab.definition: one of the two main periods of the academic year
vocab.example: He called her to say he had passed all his first-semester exams.

questions.text: What was Rustam doing at 5:50 a.m. on the station platform?
questions.hint: "He was standing on the platform at 5:50, eating a sandwich from the station café."

questions.text: Rustam had visited Almaty before this journey.
questions.hint: "He had never been to Almaty before."

questions.text: How did Apai Raushan know Rustam was nervous?
opts: She could see he was shaking
She said he was nervous on the inside
questions.correct: She said he was nervous on the inside
questions.hint: "You are on the inside" — she could see the internal nervousness even though he wasn't showing it.

questions.text: Apai Raushan's future husband was someone she met while ___ .
questions.hint: "about the friend who became her husband" — she met him as a student.

questions.text: What is the main message of the final paragraph?
opts: Exams are less important than experiences
A conversation with a stranger changed how Rustam saw himself
questions.correct: A conversation with a stranger changed how Rustam saw himself
questions.hint: "an old woman who saw something in him that he couldn't yet see in himself" — the journey changed his self-image.

questions.text: "Every journey is two journeys — the one outside and the one inside." What does this mean?
opts: You should always take two bags
External travel also involves internal change and growth
There are two types of travel
questions.correct: External travel also involves internal change and growth
questions.hint: The "inner journey" = personal development, change in perspective. Physical travel can trigger emotional/personal change.

questions.text: "His mind was racing." What does this expression mean?
opts: He was thinking very fast and couldn't stop
questions.correct: He was thinking very fast and couldn't stop
questions.hint: "mind racing" = thoughts going very fast, unable to relax. Common expression for anxiety or excitement.

questions.text: She felt ___ when she first arrived in Almaty — it was huge and frightening.
questions.hint: "overwhelming" = too much to deal with. "Overwhelmed" = the feeling of being unable to cope with something huge.

questions.text: "The train pulled into the station." What does "pull into" mean here?
questions.hint: "pull into a station" = to arrive at and stop at a station. Used for trains, buses, cars.

opts: A seat in the restaurant car
questions.hint: "berth" = a sleeping place on a train or ship. Top berth = the upper bunk. Lower berth = bottom bunk.
